questions.q: Which lipid component of the eukaryotic plasma membrane buffers membrane fluidity by preventing phospholipid fatty acid chains from packing too closely at low temperatures and restraining excessive movement at high temperatures?
questions.explain: Cholesterol inserts between phospholipid molecules in the lipid bilayer, stabilizing the membrane and moderating fluidity across temperature changes. Phosphatidylserine is an anionic phospholipid normally restricted to the inner leaflet.

open.q: Name the amphipathic sterol molecule embedded in the plasma membrane that stabilizes and regulates membrane fluidity across temperatures.

questions.q: Externalization of which phospholipid from the inner cytosolic leaflet to the outer exoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane acts as an early 'eat-me' signal for macrophages during apoptosis?
questions.explain: In healthy cells, flippases keep phosphatidylserine on the inner leaflet; during apoptosis, scramblases expose phosphatidylserine on the outer surface to trigger phagocytosis.

open.q: Which negatively charged phospholipid flips from the inner to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane to signal apoptosis to macrophages?

questions.q: What is the carbohydrate-rich coat on the external surface of the plasma membrane formed by oligosaccharide chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids called?
questions.explain: The glycocalyx (cell coat) projects from the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane and functions in cell recognition, adhesion, protection, and enzymatic digestion at the brush border.

open.q: Name the carbohydrate-rich layer covering the extracellular surface of the plasma membrane that mediates cell recognition and protection.

questions.q: Which transcriptionally active form of chromatin stains lightly under the light microscope and appears dispersed under the electron microscope?
questions.explain: Euchromatin is loosely packed, uncoiled chromatin accessible to RNA polymerase for active transcription, whereas heterochromatin is tightly condensed, darkly staining (basophilic), and transcriptionally inactive.

open.q: Which lightly staining, loosely packed form of chromatin is actively transcribed in the interphase nucleus?

questions.q: What is the primary function of the nucleolus within the interphase nucleus?
options: rRNA transcription and ribosomal subunit assembly
questions.explain: The nucleolus is a non-membrane-bound nuclear subdomain organized around nucleolar organizer regions (NORs) where rRNA genes are transcribed and combined with ribosomal proteins to form pre-ribosomal subunits.

open.q: Which macromolecular complexes are synthesized and assembled within the nucleolus of a eukaryotic cell?

questions.q: Which fibrous protein meshwork lines the inner nuclear membrane, provides structural support to the nuclear envelope, and disassembles when phosphorylated during prophase?
options: Nuclear lamina (lamins A, B, and C)
questions.explain: The nuclear lamina is composed of intermediate filament proteins called lamins (A, B, C) beneath the inner nuclear membrane; phosphorylation of lamins triggers nuclear envelope breakdown in mitosis.

open.q: Name the meshwork of intermediate filaments lining the nucleoplasmic surface of the inner nuclear membrane.

questions.q: Why does cytoplasm rich in rough endoplasmic reticulum (such as in plasma cells or pancreatic acinar cells) stain intensely basophilic with hematoxylin?
options: Abundant negatively charged phosphate groups on ribosomal RNA
High concentration of basic histone proteins
Dense bundles of eosinophilic actin filaments
questions.explain: Ribosomes studded along the rough endoplasmic reticulum contain large amounts of polyanionic rRNA, which binds basic dyes like hematoxylin (producing Nissl bodies in neurons and ergastoplasm in glandular cells).

open.q: Which nucleic acid component of ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum accounts for cytoplasmic basophilia on H&E staining?

questions.q: Which organelle is abundant in hepatocytes and steroid-secreting cells (such as Leydig cells and adrenal cortical cells) for lipid synthesis, detoxification, and calcium sequestration?
questions.explain: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes, consists of anastomosing tubules, synthesizes phospholipids and steroid hormones, detoxifies drugs via cytochrome P450 enzymes, and stores calcium ions.

open.q: Which membrane-bound tubular organelle lacking ribosomes is specialized for steroid hormone synthesis, drug detoxification, and calcium storage?

questions.q: Which face of the Golgi apparatus receives COPII-coated transport vesicles budding from the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
questions.explain: COPII vesicles transport newly synthesized proteins from transitional rER to the convex cis-Golgi network (forming face), whereas COPI vesicles mediate retrograde transport back to the rER.

open.q: Which side of the Golgi stack receives incoming transport vesicles from the rough endoplasmic reticulum?

questions.q: In I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II), failure to phosphorylate mannose residues to mannose-6-phosphate in the cis-Golgi causes acid hydrolases to be secreted outside the cell instead of being delivered to which organelle?
questions.explain: Mannose-6-phosphate tags in the Golgi direct newly synthesized acid hydrolases to mannose-6-phosphate receptors in the trans-Golgi network for packaging into clathrin-coated vesicles destined for late endosomes and lysosomes.

open.q: To which digestive organelle are proteins tagged with mannose-6-phosphate in the Golgi apparatus normally sorted?

questions.q: Which enzyme present in peroxisomes degrades toxic hydrogen peroxide into water and molecular oxygen?
questions.explain: Peroxisomes contain oxidases that generate hydrogen peroxide during beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids and catalase, which immediately decomposes hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.

open.q: Name the characteristic peroxisomal enzyme that converts hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.

questions.q: Which hydrolytic enzyme is classically used as the cytochemical marker for identifying lysosomes under light and electron microscopy?
questions.explain: Lysosomes contain roughly 40 types of acid hydrolases active at pH ~4.8-5.0; acid phosphatase is the standard histochemical marker enzyme for lysosomes, while glucose-6-phosphatase marks the endoplasmic reticulum.

open.q: Which acid hydrolase serves as the classic histochemical marker enzyme for lysosomes?

questions.q: Which phospholipid is uniquely enriched in the inner mitochondrial membrane, rendering it impermeable to ions and supporting oxidative phosphorylation complexes?
questions.explain: Cardiolipin (diphosphatidylglycerol) makes up about 20% of the inner mitochondrial membrane lipid, creating an electrical and proton barrier essential for ATP synthesis.

open.q: Name the double-phospholipid uniquely abundant in the inner mitochondrial membrane that makes it impermeable to protons and ions.

questions.q: Release of which soluble protein from the mitochondrial intermembrane space into the cytosol triggers apoptosome assembly and caspase activation during intrinsic apoptosis?
questions.explain: Permeabilization of the outer mitochondrial membrane by pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 family proteins (Bax/Bak) releases cytochrome c into the cytosol, where it binds Apaf-1 to activate procaspase-9.

open.q: Which electron-transport protein exits the mitochondrial intermembrane space into the cytoplasm to initiate the intrinsic apoptotic cascade?

questions.q: What is the characteristic cross-sectional microtubule arrangement of the axoneme in a motile cilium or flagellum?
options: 9 peripheral triplets with no central microtubules (9 + 0)
9 peripheral doublets with no central microtubules (9 + 0)
questions.explain: Motile cilia and flagella have a 9 + 2 axonemal arrangement of microtubules powered by axonemal dynein arms, whereas centrioles and basal bodies exhibit a 9 + 0 triplet arrangement.

open.q: State the microtubule arrangement found in the axoneme of a motile cilium.
accept: nine peripheral doublets and two central singlets

questions.q: A 22-year-old man presents with chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, situs inversus, and infertility due to immotile spermatozoa (Kartagener syndrome). Defect in which molecular motor protein explains his immotile cilia and flagella?
questions.explain: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) is most commonly caused by mutations in axonemal dynein arms, preventing ATP-dependent sliding between adjacent peripheral microtubule doublets.

open.q: Absence or dysfunction of which microtubule-associated motor protein causes immotile cilia and flagella in Kartagener syndrome?

questions.q: Which intermediate filament protein is characteristically expressed in epithelial cells and forms tonofilaments anchoring into desmosomes?
questions.explain: Intermediate filaments are tissue-specific: cytokeratins occur in epithelia, vimentin in mesenchymal cells, desmin in muscle, GFAP in astrocytes, and neurofilaments in neurons.

open.q: Which class of intermediate filament proteins is characteristic of epithelial cells and anchors to desmosomes?

questions.q: Which golden-brown residual body pigment accumulates in long-lived postmitotic cells such as cardiomyocytes and neurons as a sign of cellular aging ('wear-and-tear' pigment)?
questions.explain: Lipofuscin consists of indigestible oxidized lipid and protein residues within secondary lysosomes (residual bodies) and accumulates progressively with age in neurons, hepatocytes, and cardiac muscle fibers.

open.q: Name the golden-brown intralysosomal wear-and-tear pigment that accumulates in aging neurons and cardiac muscle cells.

questions.q: During which phase of the cell cycle does nuclear DNA replication and centrosome duplication occur?
questions.explain: During the S phase of interphase, the entire nuclear genome is replicated once (doubling DNA content from 2n to 4n) and the centrosome duplicates in preparation for mitosis.

open.q: In which phase of interphase does DNA synthesis take place?

questions.q: Which morphological hallmark distinguishes apoptosis (programmed cell death) from coagulative or liquefactive necrosis on histological examination?
options: Cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation and apoptotic bodies without inflammation
Cell swelling, membrane rupture and acute inflammation
Nuclear loss with preserved architecture after ischaemia
questions.explain: Apoptosis is an ATP-dependent, caspase-mediated process featuring cell shrinkage, pyknosis, karyorrhexis, and budding into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies that are rapidly phagocytosed without eliciting an inflammatory response.

open.q: Why does apoptosis fail to trigger an acute inflammatory reaction in surrounding tissue compared to necrosis?
accept: plasma membrane remains intact and apoptotic bodies are rapidly phagocytosed
intact cell membranes prevent leakage of intracellular contents
